definition: Use of generative artificial intelligence to disseminate extremist content is a field of research that examines the application of generative AI technologies (such as Viggle AI, HeyGen, and Reface) to create and spread propaganda that glorifies violence, terrorist attacks, and mass killings.
details: In 2025–2026, experts observed a trend toward using readily available AI tools to produce video content that normalizes violence and targets young audiences on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, and other social media sites.

explainer.lead: Generative tools can turn images, characters, and violent themes into media that makes attacks and mass killings look entertaining or ordinary. This matters because playful, easily shared formats can reach young audiences and normalize violence without explicitly telling viewers to kill.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a costume box that can instantly dress up horrible events as funny dances or colorful cartoons. AI-generated violent extremist content uses computer tools to do something similar, making real attackers or gruesome killings look like online entertainment. The cheerful wrapping can hide how disturbing the message is and make violence seem normal.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers studying or moderating this phenomenon must consider both generation and distribution: image-to-video systems such as Viggle AI can animate source images, while social platforms carry the resulting videos to young audiences. A key pitfall is treating dance or cartoon styling as harmless; another is assuming account suspension ends risky behavior, since Van Rootselaar opened a second ChatGPT account after being blocked.
tiers.paperLevel: A working definition is: content created with generative AI that promotes, glorifies, or normalizes violence, terrorist attacks, or mass killings, including material distributed as extremist propaganda. A 2026 Global Network on Extremism and Technology article characterized Viggle AI videos of mass murderers dancing at attack locations as normalization rather than outright incitement, within a broader 2025–2026 trend toward accessible tools and youth-targeted social distribution. The Tumbler Ridge material instead concerns AI-mediated violence-risk detection and escalation, so its planning conversations should not be conflated with generated propaganda videos.

explainer.example: In the pattern described by GNET in 2026, an image of a mass murderer is animated with Viggle AI so the killer appears to dance at the attack site, with references to the demographic targeted and the number killed. The clip does not directly urge murder, but presents a massacre as celebratory online entertainment.

usedIn.name: Viggle AI
usedIn.detail: An image-to-video platform used to animate people or fictional characters; a 2026 GNET article described its use in videos glorifying mass murderers.

usedIn.name: TikTok and Instagram
usedIn.detail: Social platforms identified in the observed 2025–2026 trend of AI-made videos normalizing violence and targeting young audiences.

usedIn.name: Extremism and technology research
usedIn.detail: Researchers examine how generative tools create and disseminate propaganda, and how entertaining aesthetics can normalize attacks.

explainer.intuition: The harm is not limited to explicit instructions to attack: entertaining or cute generated media can make real violence seem normal, celebratory, and shareable. Readily available generators allow existing images and reference videos to be repurposed into these disguised formats.
howItWorks: A creator selects a violent theme, such as an attacker, an attack location, or a targeted group.
A generative tool produces new media; Viggle AI, for example, places an image-based person or character into a reference video.
The result is packaged as entertainment, such as a dance clip or a brightly colored cartoon depicting gore.
The media circulates on social platforms, where its playful presentation can conceal its nature and help normalize violence.
explainer.whyItMatters: Such content can glorify perpetrators and normalize attacks while its cheerful appearance conceals the disturbing message. The Tumbler Ridge account also illustrates a separate governance challenge: OpenAI’s automated system and security team flagged planning activity, but management did not notify law enforcement, and a second account remained undetected until after the attack.
misconceptions: Not all such content explicitly incites violence; normalization through dance, humor, or cartoons is central.
Cartoon styling does not make content nonviolent: fruit-and-vegetable gore uses cute aesthetics to disguise torture and killings.
The Tumbler Ridge ChatGPT interactions were violence-planning conversations, not generated propaganda videos.
